appraisal_events.evidence: Legrandin eut une situation mondaine à laquelle ses relations anciennes donnèrent une sorte de solidité; couvert par le duc de Guermantes, Legrandin fut le véritable comte de Méséglise.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator narrates Legrandin's genuine rise into aristocratic legitimacy through his nephew's marriage, even seeing his self-assumed false title tacitly covered by the duc de Guermantes, while ironizing the hollow, vice-driven motives behind his long-cultivated ties.

appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte n'était que depuis peu de temps marquise de Saint-Loup (et bientôt duchesse de Guermantes); elle recevait la société la plus choisie, gardant à part les amies bourgeoises de sa mère (Bontemps, Cottard) comme indignes d'être mêlées aux gens chics.
appraisal_events.explanation: Gilberte reaches the height of aristocratic status and, for a time, visibly elevates herself above her mother's bourgeois circle by keeping them separate from her fashionable new guests.

appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte se mit à afficher son mépris pour ce qu'elle avait tant désiré, cessa de fréquenter le faubourg Saint-Germain; 'la valeur d'un titre de noblesse... monte quand on le demande et baisse quand on l'offre.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Having attained the top of the social ladder, Gilberte devalues her own hard-won prestige by scorning and abandoning the aristocracy she once craved, illustrating the narrator's explicit law that a title's worth falls as it is offered indiscriminately.

appraisal_events.evidence: La personne qui profita le moins de ces deux unions fut la jeune Mademoiselle d'Oloron qui, déjà atteinte de la fièvre typhoïde le jour du mariage religieux, se traîna péniblement à l'église et mourut quelques semaines après.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator singles her out as the one who gained least from the two marriages: gravely ill on her wedding day, she dies within weeks, a stark diminishment set against the worldly gains enjoyed by everyone else.

status_effects.explanation: His decades of quietly cultivated aristocratic ties suddenly yield a real social position, and the duc de Guermantes' cover even legitimizes his assumed title of comte de Méséglise.
The narrator ironizes his rise, tying his frenetic entrance into Charlus's circle to disreputable habits and the substitution of one 'vice' for another.
She attains the pinnacle of aristocratic status as marquise de Saint-Loup, soon duchesse de Guermantes, and briefly holds her mother's bourgeois friends at a distance from her fashionable circle.
Her name's prestige erodes at a separate, later moment as she opens her circle to all comers and spurns the aristocracy she once prized, per the narrator's stated law of status inflation.
Explicitly marked by the narrator as the one who profited least from the marriages, she dies shortly after her wedding despite the grandeur of the alliance.

ambiguities: The narrator's irony toward Legrandin's rise (retroactive false memories, a substituted rather than abandoned vice) leaves open whether the passage reads his elevation as genuine or as covert mockery.

The mourning announcement after Mlle d'Oloron's death paradoxically links Jupien's name with the greatest houses of Europe; the passage does not resolve whether this postscript is a further irony or a neutral genealogical fact.
